scenes.narration: The road from the beginning to the peak of Jesse Root Grant ran through years nobody filmed. Jesse Root Grant (January 23, 1794 – June 29, 1873) was an American farmer, tanner, and successful leather merchant who owned tanneries and leather goods shops in several different states throughout his adult life. Grant and the one who introduced Ulysses to military life at West Point.

Each stage of the life of Jesse Root Grant made the next stage possible. Jesse was born in Greensburg, Pennsylvania, and was one of seven children. At age five, Jesse moved to Ohio with his family, who settled in the Ohio River Valley.

The people who knew Jesse Root Grant young describe someone already restless. Unable to support all his children Jesse's father arranged for his apprenticeship at farms and tanneries during his youth. Jesse married Hannah Simpson Grant and they became the parents of three boys and three girls, with Ulysses being their oldest.

What Jesse Root Grant built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. Raised in a poor family that was forced to split up and having to work at an early age, Jesse persistently encouraged his sons in the ways of education, industry and hard work, his methods sometimes testing his father-son relationship with Ulysses. As a young man he worked for and came to know Owen Brown and soon acquired strong abolitionist sympathies.

By the time Jesse Root Grant reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. Jesse was known to be outspoken, had strong opinions about politics and often boasted about his son, often referring to him as "my Ulysses". Originally a Jacksonian, Jesse eventually broke with Andrew Jackson and the Democrats when developing anti-slavery leanings, and for a time wrote a number of controversial editorials in support of abolition and other issues.

The rise of Jesse Root Grant was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. He became involved in local politics and was elected mayor in Georgetown and later, Bethel, both in Ohio. During the American Civil War Jesse and two business partners became involved in cotton speculation and imposed on his son, Ulysses, to use his authority to secure early access to a portion of occupied territory.

Setbacks came early for Jesse Root Grant, and the response to them is the real story. The effort proved unsuccessful, and soon both Jesse and his business partners were sent north. Jesse stood next to his son while Ulysses was sworn in as president, thereafter becoming a frequent visitor to the White House.

The legacy of Jesse Root Grant outlived the circumstances that produced it. Much has been learned about the earlier years of Ulysses Grant from letters between father and son, as well as other source material relating to Jesse's background and business. England, aboard the Mary and John with a party of 140 emigrants who had been gathered chiefly from South West England.

Few lives travel as far as that of Jesse Root Grant, and the distance is the point. This Pilgrim party was one of many of the Puritan movement that fled England to escape religious persecution. After a 70-day journey the party arrived at Massachusetts Bay Colony in Nantasket, on May 30, 1630, and soon moved to and settled in Windsor, Connecticut.

The childhood of Jesse Root Grant contains the adult in small print. Matthew, referred to by the town folk as Honest Matthew Grant, was a highly trusted member of the community and became a surveyor and the town clerk. Later generations of the extended Grant family migrated westward into Pennsylvania, Ohio and Kentucky.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Jesse Root Grant — in that order. Jesse's grandfather Noah Grant, and his brother Solomon, fought and died in the French and Indian War, and his son, (Jesse's father) also named Noah, served in the American Revolution, including the Battle of Bunker Hill, soon advancing to the rank of captain. Grant III, was married to his first wife, Anna Richardson, who became the parents of two children, Solomon and Peter Grant.

The turning point in the life of Jesse Root Grant looked like a failure at the time. On March 4, 1792, at Greensburg, Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, Noah married his second wife, Rachael Kelly, who became Jesse's mother with the birth of her second child and first born son on January 23, 1794. Noah named Jesse after the Honorable Jesse Root, Chief Justice of the Superior Court of Connecticut.

Every biography of Jesse Root Grant has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. In 1799, when Jesse was age five, Noah moved his family to East Liverpool, and again in 1804, to Deerfield, both in Ohio. Noah worked in a shoe shop, earning a modest wage in Greensburg.

The education of Jesse Root Grant happened mostly outside any school. With little income and unable to provide enough for all his children, Noah Grant had the eleven year old Jesse apprenticed out to various families. Beginning in 1805, from 11 to 14 years old, Jesse worked in Ohio at undesignated farms earning his keep and making little extra money.

What Jesse Root Grant wanted at the start and what Jesse Root Grant got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. He didn't receive a formal education in his youth and later through years of apprenticeship became self-taught in the ways of general education and business. Placing great value on the merits of education he vowed that his sons would not have to endure the same disadvantage.

The defining trait of Jesse Root Grant was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. With no public schools in most of Ohio in the early 1800s, Jesse would later send his son Ulysses to private schools. In 1808 Jesse's father arranged for his apprenticeship with a judge, George Tod, of Youngstown, Ohio.

Those who met Jesse Root Grant at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. Jesse, age 14, lived there with his oldest sibling, Susan, while he worked under an apprenticeship that lasted four years. At the Tod residence the young Grants were treated like one of the family, where they grew to love and respect George, his wife and family.

The private years of Jesse Root Grant explain the public decades better than any speech. Jesse was sent to school three months a year, for two years. Among Jesse's playmates was the young David Tod, who would later become Governor of Ohio during the Civil War.

The family Jesse Root Grant came from matters more than the legends admit. Later in life Jesse often spoke of them in terms of affection and admiration. Working for the judge the uneducated Jesse soon learned to read and write and acquired an interest in politics, and later after he married, would even study grammar.

The first real success of Jesse Root Grant arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. A year after his commencement into apprenticeship Jesse's father Noah died, leaving him an orphan and the family very poor. At age 16 Jesse moved to Maysville, Kentucky in 1812 to work for his half brother Peter in a tannery.

The last chapter of Jesse Root Grant was written long after the fame. After completion of his training and honoring his commitment to Peter, he moved back to his boyhood town of Deerfield, Ohio, in 1815 and established his own tannery with little money, frugality and constant effort. By 1814 Jesse found employment at a tannery 15 miles away in Ravenna, Ohio, owned by the wealthy Owen Brown (father of the famous John Brown who led the raid at Harpers Ferry).

The whole life of Jesse Root Grant reads like a single decision repeated. Owen was a cattle breeder and land speculator who operated a successful tannery in Hudson, Ohio. Owen was a stout and outspoken abolitionist and Jesse often listened to his public orations against slavery, where he became familiar with and supportive of the cause.

Between the birth and the legend of Jesse Root Grant lie the years that actually decide it. During this time Jesse lived under the same roof as John Brown, became friends and came to know his abolitionist philosophy. The reputation of Jesse Root Grant was built in the middle, not at the edges. Jesse sold and shipped much of his leather to a merchant in Point Pleasant, which would become his future home in 1820. During this time Jesse took up lodging at an inn across the street from the tannery.

Somebody like Jesse Root Grant should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. Jesse's father Noah Grant died in Maysville, Kentucky, on February 14, 1819. That year, at age 25, Jesse became ill and was sent to Kentucky to recover from malaria, while his affliction sickness lasted more than a year.

The life of Jesse Root Grant begins far from where the story usually starts. Unable to work and with creditors pressing he lost most of his savings. In 1820, when he was partially recovered and able to travel short distances, he moved to Maysville and lived with relatives for several weeks.

Jesse Root Grant was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. Jesse Grant's greater family was large, residing in both Ohio and in the slave state of Kentucky. In 1820, he found work for a brief period at a tannery in Bethel, Ohio.

To understand where Jesse Root Grant ended up, start with where Jesse Root Grant began. Later that year, as an experienced tanner, he moved to Point Pleasant on the Ohio River and gained the position of foreman in a new tannery owned by Thomas Page. He soon met his future wife, Hannah Simpson, whose grandfather had arrived at Philadelphia in 1762.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Jesse Root Grant ran through years nobody filmed. On June 24, 1821, at age 27, Jesse Grant married Hannah Simpson and settled in Point Pleasant. A second son, Samuel Simpson, was born September 23, 1825, and later became a successful merchant in Galena.

Each stage of the life of Jesse Root Grant made the next stage possible. Their first daughter, Clara Rachel, was born December 11, 1828, followed by a second daughter, Virginia Paine, born February 20, 1832. By October 1823, Jesse had managed to save about $1100 (~$35,851 in 2024) to start his own tannery in Georgetown and moved the family there to start his new business.

The people who knew Jesse Root Grant young describe someone already restless. Upon arrival to Georgetown Jesse contacted the county Justice of the Peace, Thomas L. Hamer, on August 12, 1823, paid $50 and secured the deed to a lot not far from Georgetown Square.

What Jesse Root Grant built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. Here he built a two-story brick house where Ulysses, still an only child, and future brothers and sisters would be raised for the next sixteen years. On the same street he set up his tannery, a half block south from his house.

By the time Jesse Root Grant reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. Jesse also cultivated 30 acres of land while managing 50 acres of forest. With a successful business Jesse was able to pay off the deed within one year.

The rise of Jesse Root Grant was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. When his second son, Samuel Simpson, was born Jesse built one of several additions to the home, eventually doubling the size of the house. Less than a year after Jesse and Hannah were married they became the parents of their first son Ulysses, who was met with much expectation and family fanfare.
